newsitem.title: UK: City's reputation tested by Co-op takeover saga.
newsitem.headline: City's reputation tested by Co-op takeover saga.

text.p: The reputation of London's financial community is being severely tested by a controversial attempt by 31-year-old "whizz-kid" Andrew Regan to take over the venerable, mutually-owned Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS).

Regan's attempt, which collapsed on Thursday amid various court actions and an extraordinary war of words, has highlighted for some the unscrupulous side of the City and shown that the rush to do a deal could be allowed to cloud the judgement.
"During the course of the investigation we have uncovered much evidence of illegal activity and that does strike at the heart of the City," Graham Melmoth, CWS chief executive, said on Friday.

The controversy centres around confidential documents provided to Regan's bidding vehicle Galileo and his adviser, investment bank Hambros, by two senior CWS executives who have since been suspended for what the CWS called a "serious breach of trust".

In a High Court hearing on Friday a lawyer appearing for CWS read out a list of 14 financial and other institutions who had received confidential information from Hambros concerning Regan's attempt on CWS.

They included supermarkets giant J.Sainsbury, Nomura Securities, property consultant Hillier Parker, UBS, SocGen, Goldman Sachs, J.P. Morgan, Bankers Trust, HSBC Investment Bank, Lloyds Bank, Lloyds Bank Registrars and accountancy firm Price Waterhouse.

It appears that the banks on the list were approached by Regan, through Hambros, to provide financing for the deal. Most declined but Nomura was about to complete a 1.2 billion pounds ($1.9 billion) deal before it withdrew with banking sources saying it had failed to receive assurances from Galileo about the provenance of the information on CWS.

CWS chief executive Graham Melmoth has raged against the City in recent days, demanding to know why banks and others seem not to have asked enough questions about where Regan was getting his information.

The judge in Friday's hearing said the case was exceptional and represented a "gross, wilful and disgraceful breach of confidence" he also said that the way in which the information had been received was "clearly dishonest."

Banks have refused to comment publicly on their dealings with Regan and Galileo although Hambros chairman Sir Chips Keswick, a senior figure in the banking world, did write to Melmoth dismissing CWS's concerns over how the information had been obtained.

Stores group Sainsbury, approached by Regan as a possible buyer of some of the larger CWS stores, has said that it "sought and obtained assurances from Hambros that all the information provided to us had been obtained without impropriety."

Hambros, therefore seems to have been happy that since the provider of the documents, suspended CWS executive Allan Green, had handed over the information "voluntarily", that no impropriety had taken place.

Hambros is keeping a low profile on the affair but many in the City are wondering how Sir Chips would react if a senior executive at Hambros had passed confidential documents about the bank to a rival that was preparing a bid.

The affair underlines the huge difference in culture between the City, and in particular the cut-throat competition in investment banking, and an institution like the Co-op where profit is not the sole motivation.
Bill Shannon, a CWS spokesman, told Reuters on Friday that the judge's ruling and the evidence gained as a result of the court order justified its actions.

"We totally agree with what the judge said. I don't think he could have expressed it better. We made it clear in February that no part of the CWS was for sale. What we have seen is that our values and principles are not shared by some people in the City," he added.
One City source, who declined to be named, said that Hambros, which was not immediately available for comment, had acted at best "lacadaisically" over the provenance of the information.
"I think the effect on Hambros' reputation could be quite serious," the source predicted. ($ = 0.616 British Pounds)
